newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's Suharto snubs Nobel peace laureate.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Suharto snubs Nobel peace laureate.

text.p: President Suharto snubbed Nobel Peace Prize winner Bishop Carlos Belo on Tuesday during a brief visit to troubled East Timor.
The Indonesian leader twice shook hands with Belo during a ceremony in the forecourt of the governor's offices in the territory's capital Dili but did not speak to him.
But Belo, an outspoken advocate of Timorese rights, was congratulated by some of Suharto's cabinet ministers and armed forces chief General Feisal Tanjung.
Asked if he was surprised by Suharto's coolness, Belo told reporters: "I am surprised that I am congratulated by foreign people, but not from Indonesia...."
Indonesia invaded East Timor in December 1975 and annexed it the following July in a move the United Nations has refused to recognise.
Belo has served as peace-maker during sometimes brutal confrontations between the military and local activists.

Indonesia reacted with surprise to the Nobel announcement last Friday, tersely acknowledging the award to Belo but denouncing the joint award to Australia-based Jose Ramos-Horta, whom Foreign Minister Ali Alatas described as a "political adventurer".
Suharto and Belo sat side-by-side during a helicopter ride to allow Suharto to view a 27-metre (90-foot) statue of Jesus Christ erected on a headland overlooking Dili bay.

But Belo later told reporters he and the president discussed neither the Nobel award nor East Timor's political future during the 20-minute ride. He said Suharto asked him about the church and his work among the youth in East Timor.
In his Dili speech, Suharto spoke of the need for unity and stressed religious tolerance and pointedly did not mention the Nobel award.
He was speaking in mainly-Catholic East Timor at a time when Christian churches have come under attack on the most populous island of Java.
The leader of the largest Moslem group in Indonesia on Tuesday blamed the attacks on religious intolerance and told Reuters they could recur unless Moslem leaders took a firm grip on their community.

"The community should be re-oriented by its leaders towards tolerance and mutual understanding with other religions, to accept other religions and to be at home with pluralism in religion," Abdurrahman Wahid, head of the 30-million strong Nahdlatul Ulama, said.

Suharto was making his third visit to East Timor since coming to power 30 years ago. He inaugurated six public works projects covering highway, road and irrigation construction worth some $40 million.

Security was tight during the visit to prevent any pro-independence demonstration by Timorese. Troops and police lined the route from the airport to the governor's office, a two-storey white Portuguese colonial building facing the sea.
Local residents said the only trouble occurred in the morning when a group of students at the university in Dili threw stones at a passing police patrol.
In Sydney, where Ramos-Horta lives in self-imposed exile, the other Nobel laureate described the president's visit as a publicity stunt.
Asked about the joint award to Ramos-Horta, Belo told journalists: "Well, it is the decision of the Nobel committee...I have no special comment about that."
Asked if he agreed with Indonesian criticism, he added: "Most of this country, they look at Ramos-Horta as their enemy, but for me (he is) a human being and we must respect that."
